summary: Describes how servers can downgrade internationalized messages after delivery, for POP or IMAP clients that do not support Email Address Internationalization. It specifies how to present such messages to conventional clients.

eli5.summary: If a letter is written with letters your old reader cannot understand, a helper rewrites it in simpler letters before you see it.

questions: how to downgrade internationalized email for old clients
what is post delivery message downgrading
what are downgraded header fields in email
how are non-ascii email headers converted to ascii
what is an encoded-word in email
subtitle: How a POP or IMAP server rewrites internationalized email into plain ASCII headers so old clients can still read it.

tldr.problem: Internationalized messages can carry non-ASCII UTF-8 in header fields, but a POP or IMAP client that does not support that cannot be given such a message, and the server cannot safely delete it either.
tldr.mechanism: The server builds a surrogate message whose header fields are all ASCII, using encoded-words, A-labels and, as a last resort, new Downgraded- header fields that preserve the original value.
tldr.outcome: Legacy clients can display the message and tell that it was internationalized, but they cannot read it in original form and replies generally need user intervention. The RFC calls this an interim solution while clients are upgraded.

today: RFC 6857 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2013, and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. The RFC itself describes the mechanism as an interim solution while clients move to UTF-8 support, as in RFC 6855 and RFC 6856.

sections.title: The Problem with Internationalized Mail
sections.content:
Traditional mail systems, defined by the Internet Message Format, allow only ASCII characters in header field values. The SMTPUTF8 extension allows UTF-8 characters outside ASCII in those header fields. The RFC calls a string containing at least one such character a raw non-ASCII string.

If a POP or IMAP client does not send UTF8 commands or have UTF8 capability, the server cannot deliver an internationalized message to it. Because there is no standardized way to explain this to the client, the server cannot even safely discard the message. RFC 6857 fills that gap.
sections.eli5: Some emails use special letters that an old mail program cannot read. The mail server cannot hand them over and cannot throw them away, so it needs a way to help.

sections.title: The Chosen Approach: Surrogate Messages
sections.content:
The RFC lists four plausible approaches: reject the message as undeliverable, create a downgraded surrogate message that keeps as much information as possible, apply a simpler intermediate downgrade, or fabricate a message that only tells the client an internationalized message is waiting. This specification takes the second option.

None of the options preserves enough information to guarantee a reply without loss, so the RFC treats the choice as one of the "least bad" options and says the mechanism is only an interim solution while clients are upgraded. Downgrading has two parts: email header field downgrading and MIME header field downgrading. Displaying downgraded messages is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Instead of hiding the letter, the helper writes a copy that an old reader can handle, keeping as much of the message as it can.

sections.title: Rewriting Each Kind of Header Element
sections.content:
Section 3.1 defines a rewrite for each kind of ABNF element in a header field. Conversion stops when only ASCII remains.

  • Unstructured, word and comment elements: apply encoded-word encoding.
  • MIME values: remove folding whitespace outside quotes, then use extended MIME parameter encoding with the language information left empty.
  • Display names: encode as encoded-words, the same as word downgrading.
  • Domains with U-labels: rewrite them as ASCII A-labels.

For a mailbox whose local part has non-ASCII characters there is no ASCII equivalent, so the whole address is encoded as an encoded-word followed by :;, which makes the result look like an empty group. A group containing such a mailbox is rewritten as the display name, an encoded-word holding the original group list, and :;. All encoded-words use UTF-8 as their charset.
sections.eli5: Each strange word gets wrapped in a special code that old readers can pass along safely. Web addresses with fancy letters get a plain-letter version.

sections.title: Encapsulation: Downgraded Header Fields
sections.content:
As a last resort, a header field that cannot be converted is deleted and replaced by a new field named by putting Downgraded- in front of the original name. The value is treated as unstructured text and encoded-word encoded so it is entirely ASCII, and the original field is removed.

The defined names are Downgraded-Message-Id, Downgraded-Resent-Message-Id, Downgraded-In-Reply-To, Downgraded-References, Downgraded-Original-Recipient and Downgraded-Final-Recipient. Encapsulation is allowed for Message-ID:, In-Reply-To:, References:, Original-Recipient: and Final-Recipient:, and is prohibited for Received:.
sections.eli5: When a label cannot be fixed, the helper puts the original in a sealed envelope with a new label on it, so nothing is lost.

sections.title: Header Fields and MIME Parts
sections.content:
Section 3.2 gives a method for each header field in the registry. Address fields such as From:, To: and Return-Path: first get comment and display-name downgrading, then group and mailbox downgrading if non-ASCII remains. This can produce empty groups in From: and Sender:, which RFC 6854 allows.

In Received:, domains and comments are downgraded, and a FOR clause with a non-ASCII local part, or an ID clause with a non-ASCII value, is removed. Subject:, Comments: and Content-Description: use unstructured downgrading. Unknown fields, including List- fields, get unstructured downgrading unless the software knows a better algorithm and SHOULD use it.

MIME body part header fields are checked at all levels of the MIME structure and treated like the same-named top-level fields. In a delivery status notification, non-ASCII Original-Recipient: and Final-Recipient: fields get type-addr downgrading.
sections.eli5: The helper goes through the letter one line at a time, fixing each line in the way that suits it, including lines inside attachments.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Receivers can tell a message was internationalized, but cannot read it in original form and generally cannot reply without significant user intervention. Rewriting header fields increases opportunities for undetected spoofing by malicious senders, though the rewritten values are kept in MIME form or in new fields traditional clients do not process.

Downgrading may break signature methods, likely including DKIM and possibly S/MIME and PGP. The mechanism SHOULD NOT remove signatures even if they will fail, and SHOULD preserve as much information as possible. Clients may use an Authentication-Results header field to judge whether signatures were valid before downgrading. The Downgraded-* fields are not inspected by traditional clients and may be less trustworthy than the traditional fields.
sections.eli5: Changing a letter can break its seal, so old seals may look broken. Keep the seal anyway, and be careful trusting the sealed envelopes.

sections.title: Encoding Notes and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC warns that some deployed implementations handle whitespace between adjacent encoded-words incorrectly, so behavior is somewhat unpredictable. Although RFC 5322 says lines SHOULD be 78 characters or less, implementations MAY allow overly long encoded words to work around faulty software, and SHOULD then offer an optional way to limit line length to 78 characters.

The experimental Downgraded-* fields from RFC 5504 are no longer in use, and IANA changed their status to obsoleted. The six new fields in section 3.1.10 were registered, except that the registration list names five of them and omits Downgraded-Resent-Message-Id.
sections.eli5: Some old programs get confused by the coded words, so the rules allow a few workarounds. The old experimental labels were retired and new ones were registered.
